competitors.title: Why Your Agent Needs a Credential Broker - Introducing CB4A
key_points: CB4A (Credential Broker for Agents) is an IETF Internet-Draft specifying a credential vaulting and brokering architecture where agents never hold real long-lived credentials
TeamPCP LiteLLM compromise in March 2026 exposed 300GB of credentials affecting 500,000 corporate identities — the canonical example of why credential brokering is needed
Architecture separates Policy Decision Point (PDP) from Credential Delivery Point (CDP) — compromise one does not give you the other
Builds on SPIFFE/SPIRE for workload identity, DPoP (RFC 9449) for sender-constrained token binding, and NIST SP 800-207 PDP/PEP separation
Three proxy models: Proxy Gateway (transparent injection), Short-Lived Token Minting (time-limited tokens), Credential Wrapping (encrypted to target service)
Includes tiered approval framework with human-in-the-loop support and 11 identified threats with mitigations

competitors.title: Agent credential brokers in 2026: Authsome vs Agent Vault vs Clawvisor vs OneCLI
key_points: Four open-source credential brokers compared: Authsome (local-first Python CLI, 44 bundled OAuth2 providers), Agent Vault (Go binary, multi-tenant, separate host), Clawvisor (authorization gateway with task-scoped human approval), OneCLI (Rust HTTP gateway with Bitwarden integration)
All four share the same premise: the agent should not hold real credentials; all use proxy intercept on outbound HTTP to substitute placeholders with real keys
Authsome best for solo developers on laptops; Agent Vault/OneCLI for production fleets; Clawvisor for high-stakes approval flows
Three open questions: who owns OAuth2 refresh, whether proxy needs to be on agent host, and whether brokering alone is enough vs needing authorization layers
Recommended combination: Authsome on dev laptops, Agent Vault/OneCLI in production, Clawvisor as optional approval layer for high-blast-radius operations

competitors.title: AI agent security - IBM Think
key_points: AI agent security covers expanded attack surface, autonomous actions at speed, unpredictable inference, and lack of transparency
Key vulnerabilities: prompt injection, tool/API manipulation, data poisoning, memory poisoning, privilege compromise, authentication spoofing, RCE, cascading failures
Best practices: zero trust architecture, principle of least privilege, context-aware authentication, data encryption, microsegmenting, prompt hardening, prompt validation
Only 29% of organizations deploying agentic AI report being prepared to secure those deployments
Prompt injection appeared in 73% of production AI deployments in 2025

competitors.title: AI agent governance - IBM Think
key_points: AI agents present unique governance challenges due to autonomy, adaptability, and complexity
Key challenges: lack of human control, opacity of decision-making, bias amplification, security vulnerabilities, API integration risks
Solutions: AI sandboxing for pre-deployment testing, agent-to-agent monitoring, governance agents that monitor other agents, emergency shutdown mechanisms
Organizations need scalable governance models, strong cybersecurity protocols, and human-in-the-loop oversight

competitors.title: AI Credential Theft 2026: Why Honeytokens Beat Traditional Defenses
key_points: Credential theft surged 160% in 2025, driven by AI-powered infostealers that bypass EDR and MFA
Honeytokens provide zero-false-positive detection — any access to a honeytoken is guaranteed malicious
Honeytokens are more effective than traditional defenses against AI-driven credential theft because attackers cannot distinguish them from real credentials
Canary tokens and honey tokens are essential deception technology for detecting AI agent credential compromise

competitors.title: Agentic AI Security in 2026: Prompt Injection, Tool Hijacking, and the Defense Stack
key_points: The 2025-2026 shift from conversational AI to agentic AI fundamentally changed the threat landscape
Agents operate with real-world permissions, hold credentials, maintain persistent memory, and chain multi-step actions across tools
When an AI agent can browse the web, execute code, send emails, query databases, and call external APIs, a successful prompt injection is a full system compromise
The gap between capability deployment and security readiness is the defining risk of the agentic era
